Muscle fibers don't burn fat at all. Ever. What's going on is that muscles burn ATP when used, creating a large amount of cyclic AMP. This triggers an intracellular signaling cascade that results in glucose transporters being placed on the cell surface, allowing the muscles to draw sugar directly out of the bloodstream without the presence of insulin. This means that muscles are able to take up sugar whenever they need it, so it's an effective way to lower blood glucose for diabetics. (Strangely enough, exercise also makes the body more responsive to insulin, so a lower dose is required to have the same effect. This is why it's so important for type 2 diabetics to exercise.)

Low blood glucose results in the release of glucagon from pancreatic alpha cells. Glucagon causes the liver to produce glucose through glycogenolysis (breakdown of stored glycogen) and gluconeogenesis (production of glucose from other sources like fatty acids, lactate, pyruvate, and amino acids). Fatty acids are released into the blood by adipose cells in response to low levels of insulin, which is a result of low blood sugar from exercising or not eating, and are the main source of the precursors used in gluconeogenesis. Adipose is actually burned long before muscle tissues, despite what you see on a lot of websites. Protein is one of the last sources used due to the amount of energy it takes to convert it to a useable form and the number of byproducts produced in their metabolism.
